![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47158642/220197588-25e11022-02e4-45f3-b2e5-392c4ce7a025.png)

Huge credit to @StarLederer, who did almost all of the work on this. We're just reusing this PR to keep everything in one place.

# Objective

1. Make bloom more physically based.
1. Improve artistic control.
1. Allow to use bloom as screen blur.
1. Fix #6634.
1. Address #6655 (although the author makes incorrect conclusions).

## Solution

1. Set the default threshold to 0.
2. Lerp between bloom textures when `composite_mode: BloomCompositeMode::EnergyConserving`.
1. Use [a parametric function](https://starlederer.github.io/bloom) to control blend levels for each bloom texture. In the future this can be controlled per-pixel for things like lens dirt.
3. Implement BloomCompositeMode::Additive` for situations where the old school look is desired.

## Changelog

* Bloom now looks different.
* Added `BloomSettings:lf_boost`, `BloomSettings:lf_boost_curvature`, `BloomSettings::high_pass_frequency` and `BloomSettings::composite_mode`.
* `BloomSettings::scale` removed.
* `BloomSettings::knee` renamed to `BloomPrefilterSettings::softness`.
* `BloomSettings::threshold` renamed to `BloomPrefilterSettings::threshold`.
* The bloom example has been renamed to bloom_3d and improved. A bloom_2d example was added.

## Migration Guide

* Refactor mentions of `BloomSettings::knee` and `BloomSettings::threshold` as `BloomSettings::prefilter_settings` where knee is now `softness`.
* If defined without `..default()` add `..default()` to definitions of `BloomSettings` instances or manually define missing fields.
* Adapt to Bloom looking visually different (if needed).

Also as a response to that, but separately from my previous comment, I'd like to propose a physically based technique to artistically control bloom that replaces threshold. Since bloom is the effect of light scattering in the lens, and our goal is to be able to "tighten" the effect, I think we can achieve that by tinting the lens and increasing the exposure. That way the light that travels through the lens more will loose energy while the photons that go straight through are brought back to their initial luminance by the increased exposure.

Of course, implementing that directly will result in large number multiplications and loss of color precision so instead we can simply tint the color at downsampling stage which will result in the same output

These spheres have emissive materials with 5-500 units of radiance per channel. They get clipped in SDR rendering so they are not going to look as glowy. Clipping happens before the image gets to the post-processing effects so all our effect "sees" is dim white spheres, our effect doesn't know they are supposed to be very bright and colorful.

I am actually surprised some color does get through... perhaps the material shaders apply the ACES-RRT-like function you implemented themselves when rendering to an SDR target? If that is the case that makes no sense physically and makes the bloom effect weirder than it could be... Regardless, there is no way around clipping, if it occurs, your scene is not going to look natural. ~~There is a technique that I tried a while ago that sacrificed color precision for more dynamic range and it worked surprisingly well but that's a story for another day.~~

I don't think there is anything off about the bloom effect when in SDR it's just limitations of SDR.

Oh yeah, when not using HDR, tonemapping is applied in the main PBR shader, before bloom. That's a problem. Not sure how we fix that. Do we need to support bloom with SDR textures? I guess we could always use a separate tonemap node when BloomSettings is a component on the view, hmm. I'll think about it tomorrow.

Also, I just realized, we're going to have a hard time supporting WebGL. We can use separate textures in place of mips, but we can't use hdr, which is a bigger problem.

> when not using HDR, tonemapping is applied in the main PBR shader, before bloom

This is actually very nice because this way we can have some post-processing effects without actually doing post-processing (e.g. tone-mapping, color-correction, vignette). However, this can put actual post-processing effects in a weird position. Ideally in-material "post-processing" should be configurable so that users can disable it when using actual post-processing or even use a combination of the two (I'd personally do vignette in PBR shader, then bloom and tonemapping in post-processing). It is also going to be extremely easy to implement my ~~secret technique~~ dynamic range compression technique that I mentioned in the other post with this setup.

I guess you could argue that the main PBR shader is already customizable because you can always just copy core bevy code into your source directory and modify it (aka reason I love Bevy so much) and honestly, I'd argue this point, but it is probably best to have a `linear_output` toggle on the PBR system instead of relying on `camera.hdr` to determine user's intentions.

> We can use separate textures in place of mips, but we can't use hdr, which is a bigger problem

Anyway, additive bloom can still make artistic sense in SRD, and in very dim scenes even energy-conserving bloom is possible. We do currently use HDR textures internally regardless of how the camera is configured but that can be changed using pipeline specialization, that way we can make WebGL work

WebGL2. Apparently there are issues with linear textures and MSAA on WebGL2, which is why it's not on by default :/

I might be wrong about some of this but I have done research on the topic before too. Here is my understanding:

In an ideal ACES workflow you perform your shading calculations in ACES AP0 color space (or more commonly in linearazed sRGB colorspace and map to AP0 just before tone-mapping) and, when it's time to output, you apply the Reference Rendering Transform (RRT), followed by an Output Device Transform (ODT) that corresponds to the output device and in some cases even the surroundings (how the room is lit). Of course, most of the time it is not really worth it and you just hardcore everything together into a function that combines conversion from (hopefully) linearized sRGB to ACES AP0, RRT and sRGB ODT. [Unity does pretty much that](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/Graphics/blob/d8d526b8fd5e7c85c1981eb171d4a505668deb19/Packages/com.unity.render-pipelines.core/ShaderLibrary/Color.hlsl#L642), unfortunately their (very good) implementation is under [this sketchy license](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/Graphics/blob/master/Packages/com.unity.render-pipelines.core/LICENSE.md) so I don't know if we can just copy it. Unity Core Rendering Pipeline also includes [a spec-compliant implementation](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/Graphics/blob/d8d526b8fd5e7c85c1981eb171d4a505668deb19/Packages/com.unity.render-pipelines.core/ShaderLibrary/ACES.hlsl) which is under a free license (see file) but it is probably slower. I don't think this is much better than what @JMS55 already implemented. It looks like it is just the S curve without the glow module, red transform and global desaturation. That function will never look AAA, creates visual artifacts with very bright and very saturated colors, and blocks us from supporting HDR (or any non sRGB) display in the future.

> I think over-complicating things for the sake of accuracy won't be of much use for most bevy users

It's not for the sake of accuracy, ACES RRT is is what the greatest color grading experts concluded looks best and I think it's smart to use their expertise [The Academy](https://www.oscars.org/) made available for free. A proper ACES tonemap is not that complex if you look at [their reference implementation](https://github.com/ampas/aces-dev) (which i probably should have mentioned instead Unity), all you need is to be in ACES AP0 which is achieved by a simple matrix multiplication, then execute [this (RRT)](https://github.com/ampas/aces-dev/blob/dev/transforms/ctl/rrt/RRT.ctl), then [this (ODT)](https://github.com/ampas/aces-dev/blob/dev/transforms/ctl/odt/rec709/ODT.Academy.Rec709_D60sim_100nits_dim.ctl) if you target normal monirots or [this (ODT)](https://github.com/ampas/aces-dev/blob/dev/transforms/ctl/odt/rec2020/ODT.Academy.Rec2020_100nits_dim.ctl) if you target HDR ones.

We can technically improve performance by converting everything in RRT to work on lineraized sRGB but that is a lot of work and technical debt. Alternatively, we can bring the entire color workflow into ACES (textures need to be converted to ACES AP0 instead of linear sRGB) upon load. Or at least I would just follow the steps I mention above.

@StarLederer Sometime soon, I plan to remove the SDR stuff and rebase the code so that we can merge this in time for bevy 0.10. I'll fork it into a separate branch first, in case you want to add back SDR support in the future.

> This has issues when running on DX12 due to `BloomUniforms` not being mapped.

What does this mean? "Not being mapped"? Does it mean not bound? Though the errors are from naga...

This is quite a big PR with multiple things being changed at once. That makes review more difficult as the context is "do things to make bloom better" rather than "address this one issue with bloom" and a series of PRs like that that are small, clear, and easy to review. Each of the points in the solutions section in the description look to be logically-separate concerns.

And to be clear, I know it is difficult to know what ideas are going to produce good results and not when working on rendering code and you have to put a lot of things into place to find out what ideas you want to keep and what you want to remove. That leads to branches with multiple features implemented on top of each other and that perhaps interact with each other. However, when it comes to reviewing, it is important to keep things as small as one can. I myself have gone through the process of splitting out bits and pieces from branches I've hacked on for the sake of making reviewing easier. I'd strongly encourage this approach and more things will get merged more quickly by doing things this way.

EDIT: I just realised that an example is that my current focus has been on reviewing PRs but my next coding effort is going to be to start making small, focused PRs out of my batching hack branch.

> in case you want to add back SDR support in the future

I thought that'd be a sure thing. I was procrastinating disabling HDR support myself mainly because it is the comments that need to be changed and not code.

I also agree with @superdump. One more advantage of doing things that way is that it makes it easier to rebase (e.g. I had to resolve tonemapping related conflicts in the PBR shader when working on bloom)

Fixed all the references. I'm unsure how the slide numbers got messed up, but I've corrected them against the reference link I put in the shader.

Also fixed the 0.25, thanks for noticing. No wonder bloom looked weird to me yesterday when I was testing something :P.

All that's remaining is double checking the LearnOpenGL article we're basing our code off of is correct. I've left those discussions up for now.

I've gone through the shader parts of the learnopengl article and compared. I also checked the sampler and texture configurations. I haven't checked the rest of the GL API code as I'm more confident about the data flow already.

The only thing I noticed that was 'missing' was the 'Bonus Material 0: Graphical Debugging' part about the black boxes. The solution to that problem was to add a `max(sample, 0.0001)` at the end of the first downsample pass to make sure no multiply by zeros were introduced that propagate into black boxes. I don't know if we've experienced that at all or if it doesn't happen for some other small detail in what we have implemented. Instead we seem to clamp between 0.0 and what looks to be possibly the largest representable float. I think I'll add in the 0.0001 as the lower bound of the clamp, for safety.
Removed the ACES change. Left a comment in the BloomSettings docs to suggest a good tonemapper.

Some of the bloom “shapes“ now seem to be duplicated/triplicated horizontally for me, is this due to the firefly prevention mechanism? ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/418473/219893163-266ffe68-e672-4162-b00f-3a46cd778866.png)

The examples are currently broken, I get an error about `view` not being in scope when enabling a different tonemapper.
`color = saturation(color, view.color_grading.pre_saturation);`

EDIT: Fixed

@robtfm came up with a great improvement to make bloom look more consistent at various resolutions.

 The only thing really missing now is the glowing bevy logo in the bloom_2d example looks kinda bad. Rather than adjust the color values in code, it would be better to encode the image such that the white birds are bright, but the black circle they are on aren't. The way it is now, the whole thing kinda fades to white and looks bad and washed out. Not a huge blocker though, and we could just remove it. We've had questions in the past on how to add bloom to a 2d sprite, so that was my attempt at trying to show it. Didn't work out that well.

> this might be a problem for dynamic upsizing

Bloom will run after those at display resolution. It's only the prepass/main pass/etc that render at a reduced resolution.

issue_context.body:
## Bevy version 0.9

## What you did

Combined the [transparent_window](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/blob/main/examples/window/transparent_window.rs) example with the [bloom](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/blob/main/examples/3d/bloom.rs) example. (I'm only using this to quickly test the alpha as my actual use case was much more complex)

## What went wrong

There is transparency across the frame, even if the background if opaque.

With default clear color:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33357138/201998453-d5c114c5-fdd8-4b05-95d6-316b24ae08ec.png)

With `ClearColor(Color::NONE)`:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33357138/201998752-ad9b628b-ee7a-4562-84e8-e41f456d9366.png)

review_comments: Is this because we're reading from/writing to different mip levels?

Sorta. You only need post_process_write() when you want to both read and write from the view target in the _same_ pass. In this render node, we split the work over multiple render passes, first reading from the view target, then writing to some intermediary mips of a different texture, and then writing the result to the view target. So there's no need for post_process_write().
This seems oddly-named given the description...
Could use a small doc comment
